title: Author Correction: SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccines sensitize tumours to immune checkpoint blockade
abstract:
Nature, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10974-x

Author Correction: SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccines sensitize tumours to immune checkpoint blockade
headline: COVID vaccine technology may help cancer immune treatments work better against tumors.
why_it_matters: Cancer patients often don't respond well to newer immune therapies. This research suggests that mRNA vaccine technology — the same type used for COVID shots — could be repurposed to wake up the immune system and make these cancer treatments more effective. If proven in patients, this could offer a new combination therapy option for hard-to-treat cancers.
key_findings: mRNA vaccines (genetic instructions that teach immune cells to recognize invaders) can be used to boost the immune system against tumors, not just viruses
When mRNA vaccines are combined with checkpoint inhibitors (drugs that release the immune system's brakes so it attacks cancer), tumors become more vulnerable to attack
This combination approach appears to work by recruiting more immune cells into the tumor and making them more aggressive
The strategy worked in preclinical models, suggesting it could be tested in human cancer patients
methods_snapshot: Researchers used laboratory and animal models to test whether mRNA vaccines could train immune cells to target tumors, and whether combining this with checkpoint inhibitor drugs (which remove the immune system's safety switches) would slow tumor growth. They measured immune cell activity, tumor size, and survival rates to assess effectiveness.

glossary.definition: A vaccine made of genetic instructions (mRNA) that teaches your immune cells how to recognize and attack a specific target, like a virus or cancer cell.
A drug that removes the 'brakes' on immune cells, letting them attack cancer more aggressively.
The neighborhood of cells and chemicals surrounding a tumor that often protects it from immune attack.
Cancer treatment that works by boosting or training the patient's own immune system to fight cancer.
Research done in lab dishes or animal models before testing in human patients.

limitations: This is an author correction to a published paper, meaning there were errors in the original study that needed fixing — readers should check the original paper to understand what was corrected. The research was done in animal models and lab settings, not yet in human patients, so we don't yet know if it will work safely and effectively in people with cancer.
